title: Handprints to Decorate Our Room
strapline: Every child's hand on the wall — the room becomes ours because we made it.
intent: Children develop a sense of belonging by putting something of themselves permanently into the room.
Seeing every hand together — different sizes, different skin colours, all on one display — makes difference ordinary and visible.
The whole-hand, whole-arm movement of printing builds gross and fine motor control.
Waiting for a turn at the paint tray builds patience and turn-taking early in the year.
Children experience their own contribution mattering to a shared space.
implementation: Model the whole process first, slowly, so children know exactly what will happen to their hands.
Offer a genuine range of paint colours — including a range of skin tones — and let each child choose.
Let children press their own hand down rather than pressing it for them; the print is theirs.
Have warm water and towels immediately to hand for children who dislike the sensation.
Accept a fingerprint, a thumbprint or a brush-painted hand from any child who does not want a full print.
Label each print with the child's own name card so they can find themselves.
Hang the display at child height, where they can reach and revisit it all year.
key_questions: Which colour will you choose for your hand?
How does the paint feel on your skin?
Can you find your own handprint on our wall?
Whose hand is bigger than yours? Whose is smaller?
What shall we call our display?

impact.text: Children feel pride and ownership in a room they helped make.
Children take a turn and wait for others without the wait spoiling it.
Children make a real choice of colour and own the result.
Children compare sizes — bigger, smaller, same — using their own hands.
Children notice that hands and skin differ, and treat that as ordinary.
Children manage the messy business of painting and washing with growing independence.

enhancements: A handprint tree or wreath that grows as new children join through the year.
A second print in the summer term, mounted beside the first, to show how much they have grown.
A family handprint session so parents' and siblings' hands join the display.
A footprint version outdoors on paving slabs or a long roll of paper.
A name-writing extension — children label their own print as their writing develops.
A skin-tone mixing table where children mix a colour that matches their own hand.

playing_exploring: Children explore paint with their whole hand, a sensory experience in itself.
Choosing a colour and pressing down is an open, low-risk invitation to have a go.
active_learning: Children wait, take their turn and see it through to a finished print.
They return to the display again and again to find themselves in it.
creating_thinking: Children make deliberate choices about colour and placement.
Comparing hands prompts thinking about size, difference and belonging.
